title: Compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday, a God who suffers: Jesus weeping near the tomb of his friend. Your line was god in the pain.

A funeral is coming out through the gate of a town called Nain. A young man is being carried out on a bier. Luke gives the detail that makes it unbearable: he was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." A crowd from the town walks with her. Coming up the road the other way is Jesus, with his own crowd. Two processions meet at the gate. Nobody asks him for anything. Luke says that when he saw her, something moved in him before he said a word or lifted a hand.
screen: `A FUNERAL AT THE GATE OF NAIN.`

segments.voice: Some readers hear two Latin pieces inside the English word compassion: with, and suffering. Suffer with: not pity handed down, but feeling it from beside. The Gospels' word goes lower still: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." The Greek verb is splanchnizomai, and some readers hear in it the gut: being moved in your insides. You met that gut-deep word back on day one hundred eighty-three, with a crowd like sheep without a shepherd. Luke uses it of the Samaritan who stops for the man left half dead on the Jericho road: "he had compassion on him." And of the father in the parable of the lost son: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Notice the order. The feeling comes first, then the body moves. Jesus touches the bier, and the young man sits up. The Samaritan goes to him and binds up his wounds. The father runs. Compassion here isn't a mood; it ends in the hands and feet. Last, Paul makes it a job for ordinary people: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." And: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." Some Christians link it to yesterday: if God suffers with people, following him means doing the same. It doesn't answer why there is suffering. It answers a different question: what now?

Choose someone hurting whom you could actually reach, and picture the conversation: notice the pull to keep it short, to cheer them up, to fix it, and picture yourself staying instead, listening longer than is comfortable, letting a silence sit. If you pray, you can bring them to God; if you don't, let the picture of staying be enough for now. And if they ever say they're in danger, in the US you can call or text 988 together, or reach local emergency help.
Compassion. Suffering with someone: being moved inside, and then staying close.
Your line: suffer with. Feeling first, then the hands. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians practice compassion by visiting the sick and grieving, bringing meals, sitting with the dying and giving to those in need; churches organize care teams, hospital chaplaincies and works of mercy.

chat.says: My friend is really sad. Should I just cheer her up fast so she feels better?
options: Maybe stay with her instead: compassion means suffering with, weeping with those who weep.
Yes, cheering up fast is compassion; staying in someone's sadness only makes it worse.
Just feel sorry for her quietly; compassion is a private feeling, not something you do.
chat.meaning: In Luke, compassion is feeling first, then hands and feet. Paul says weep with them that weep: staying close, not fixing fast.

notes: The Latin 'with + suffering' reading of 'compassion' is attributed to 'some readers', under the claims rule; the index hook states it as the meaning. Confirm.
splanchnizomai and its link to splanchna (inward parts) attributed to 'lexicons'; confirm. Confirm Luke uses the same verb at 7:13, 10:33 and 15:20.
Hook: 'Nobody asks him for anything' reflects Luke 7:11–13, where no request is recorded; confirm.
The Samaritan is named without the priest and Levite, to avoid using them as a foil.
